runs.text: Tirar fruito, & proueito como de prègação, ou

lines.note: Continues the preceding entry: drawing fruit or benefit from preaching or a lesson. The scan supports Tirar and proueito, replacing the OCR forms Titar and proucio; the historical fruito remains unchanged.
Lição completes the preceding comparison, identifying a lesson as another source of benefit. This short continuation remains a separate printed row.
Toriagari gives principal forms of rising or climbing to a high place. The Portuguese comparison continues with a fortress on the next line.
A fortaleza completes the example of ascending to an elevated place; it belongs to toriagari, not the following verb.
Toriague means taking and lifting something. The printed uru ending belongs to the historical verb paradigm and is preserved.

runs.text: algũa couſa. ¶ Item, Tirar o cargo, ou rẽ-

lines.note: After completing the lifting sense, the gloss gives removal of an office or income. Tirar is wholly Portuguese italic, and the abbreviated rẽ- continues as renda below.
The examples concern taking away yaku, an office, or chigyoo, an income or holding. The scan shows initial Y in Yacu, not OCR Vacu; the final to- continues the verb on the next row.
Riaguru completes toriaguru. The next example, ko wo toriaguru, introduces taking a newborn into one's arms; Tomar is entirely within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: criança nos braços quãdo nace, em ſinal q̃ a to-

lines.note: The child is taken into the arms at birth as a sign of accepting responsibility. The abbreviation q̃ and following article a are separately printed; the last to- continues tomar.

runs.text: ma a cargo como padrinho, ou madrinha.

lines.note: Completes tomar a cargo: assuming responsibility as godfather or godmother. The note describes the dictionary's comparison without changing its wording.
Toriaguevoya is the person who receives the newborn, rendered here as godfather or godmother. The compound retains its printed internal v.

runs.text: tomão a criança nos braços quando nace.

lines.note: The relative clause completes the preceding definition: those who take the child in their arms when it is born. The printed tomão is retained.
Toriai means struggling or contending with one another. The first letter is T, matching the following tor- entries, rather than OCR F; both principal-form vowels carry carons.

runs.text: ſi: no negatiuo ſignifica não ter deuer, ou não ſe

lines.note: The definition turns from mutual contention to the negative construction, explained as not acknowledging an obligation or not responding. The colon after ſi is visible in the scan.
Dar por achado completes the idiom for taking notice. Nanto mooshitemo begins the example: no matter what one says; the divided to- belongs to toriauanu below.

runs.text: He homem que por mais q̃

lines.note: Toriawanu hito ja describes someone who will not engage or take notice. The Portuguese introduces a relative clause saying that however much he is told, he remains unaffected.

runs.text: lhe digão não ſe lhe dà nada.

lines.note: Completes the example: however much people tell him, he does not care. The Portuguese dative construction supplies the sense of the negative toriauanu.
Toriarashi describes taking things while leaving disorder behind. The principal part aita reflects the historical s-verb inflection; Tomando is wholly italic.

runs.text: deixar o mais deſmanchado, & botado por ahi.

lines.note: The rest is left dismantled and thrown about. The scan separates por ahi; no modernization of the historical adverb ahi is introduced.
Ie no shozaimotsu wo toriarasu illustrates plundering the belongings of a house. The bare t in xozaimotuo is retained rather than expanding the Japanese spelling; Rou- begins roubando.

runs.text: bando o fato da caſa deixar o pior por ahi eſpa-

lines.note: The Portuguese explains taking household goods and leaving the worse items scattered about. The scan supports ahi, with h, rather than OCR abi; eſpa- continues espalhado.
Completes espalhado and adds desbaratado, scattered and disordered. The round s in the retained desbaratado is not normalized to a long s.
Toriatari means receiving or coming out by lot. The initial is a capital T, and the Portuguese ſor- belongs to sortes on the next row.
Kuji ni toriataru specifies obtaining something through a lot; Idem refers back to the same meaning. The divided Portuguese tes closes sortes.
Toriatsukai means negotiating or handling a matter. The paired ǒ and ǒta forms retain the visible carons.
Kuji wo toriatsukoo concerns handling a lawsuit or dispute, as made explicit by demanda below. The printed long-vowel form is preserved.
After completing the lawsuit sense, ie no saiban wo begins a new example about household administration. The object and its verb span two physical lines.
The verb completes the household-management example. Portuguese entender no negocio means attending to affairs; me- is the beginning of meneo below.
Meneo and governo explain the running or administration of the house. This is the continuation of the preceding gloss, not another headword.
Toriatsume means gathering things by taking them with the hand. The printed initial is T rather than OCR r, and cõ is an unexpanded abbreviation for com.
Takara wo toriatsumuru gives accumulation of wealth as the example. The isolated italic A- starts Ajuntar on the following physical row.
Completes Ajuntar muitas riquezas, gathering many riches. It directly translates the preceding Japanese example.
Toriawase means bringing different things together to see how they match. The principal forms are copied as printed; the Portuguese cou- continues cousas.

runs.text: ſas, & prouar ſe fazem, ou ſão proporciona-

lines.note: The gloss specifies testing whether the things fit or are proportionate. The divided proporciona- continues across the physical line boundary.

runs.text: das, como o forro do vestido com aparte de fora

lines.note: The example compares a garment lining with its exterior. Printed aparte is retained as the close-set article and noun rather than silently regularized.

runs.text: ou de cima. ¶ Item, Ajuntar duas peßoas

lines.note: After completing the garment comparison, the entry introduces bringing two people together. The following line specifies the purpose as marriage.
The example joins a woman to a husband in marriage. Vottoni and vonnauo retain their printed initial v forms, and tori- continues the verb below.
Awasuru completes toriawasuru in the preceding matchmaking example. This short Japanese-only continuation is a separate physical row.
The noun toriawase is also explained as intercession. A separate example begins with the noun and object particle; the capital T replaces OCR r.
Suru completes toriawase wo suru, directly translated as interceding. The short row closes the preceding noun entry.
Toriawasete names an intercessor or intermediary. The Portuguese terceiro describes a third party acting between others.

runs.text: O aleuantar os calções, ou arre-

lines.note: Toribakama is raising or hitching up the breeches. The Portuguese arre- continues arregaçar-se on the next line.
The gloss specifies hitching the clothing up somewhat. Toribakama wo su- begins the corresponding Japanese expression with suru divided over the row boundary.
Ru completes suru; Idem directs the reader back to the same clothing action. The brief continuation is preserved independently.

runs.text: Vaſo como barça de vinho que tem dã-

lines.note: Toribe is a vessel compared with a wine container. The abbreviated dã- continues dambas, describing features on both sides.

runs.text: bas as partes como aſas por onde ſe toma.

lines.note: The vessel has handle-like projections on both sides by which it is held. Bas completes the preceding abbreviated dambas.

Toribishio denotes a preparation of birds cut into small pieces. The scan supports Toribixiuo and feitos em, replacing corrupted OCR; po- continues postos at the top of the next column. The supplied NINJAL v202510 headword index corroborates the independently read headword.

runs.text: ſtos de molho em hũa certa ſalmoura pera depo-

lines.note: Stos completes postos from the bottom of column 1. The pieces of bird are put to soak in a particular brine, with depois divided at this line end.
Is completes depois: the salted preparation is to be eaten later. This closes the Toribixiuo entry carried across the column boundary.

runs.text: Modo de telhar com taboinhas lar-

lines.note: Toribuki is roofing with small broad boards. A visible terminal hyphen, rather than the OCR period, joins lar- to largas below.

runs.text: gas ſem as pregar com pregos. Vt,

lines.note: The broad boards are laid without fastening them with nails. Toribuki- begins the Japanese example across the line boundary.
Toribuki ni suru means roofing in the manner just described. The Japanese continuation and Portuguese infinitive are in their respective typefaces.
Torikakari means beginning to do something. The Portuguese has a visible space in a fazer; the example follows below.
Gakumon ni torikakaru means beginning study, exactly matching começar a estudar. The attached particle ni is preserved in the printed form.
The entry also gives the sense of attacking or rushing at something. This is an additional meaning of torikakari, not a separate headword.
Torikakomi means surrounding a person or place. The mark over the principal part is visibly a circumflex, ôda, rather than the OCR caron.
A fortress or house supplies examples of the objects that can be surrounded. The row completes the previous definition.
Torikakushi is taking a thing and concealing it. The printed eſcon- continues escondela; the OCR eſcom- is not supported by the final n shape.

runs.text: dela. ¶ Item, Enterrar o corpo morto. Vt,

lines.note: After completing escondela, the gloss adds burial of a dead body. Corpo is one word in the scan, correcting the OCR split cor po.
Shigai wo torikakusu gives the dead-body example for concealing or burying. The Japanese phrase is a complete separate physical row.
Torikaji denotes the port side. The scan prints the historical Portuguese form Bumbordo, with u; the example begins fune wo torikaji ni yaru, and its divided fragment is torica-.

runs.text: Nauegar, ou fazer ir a embar-

lines.note: Gini yaru completes the instruction to send the vessel toward port. The Portuguese embar- continues embarcação below.

runs.text: cação pera a parte de bombordo que he a parte

lines.note: The vessel is directed to the port side. This occurrence prints bombordo with o, contrasting with Bumbordo in the short gloss above; both forms are retained.

runs.text: eſquerda, eſtando virado pera a proa. ¶ Vo-

lines.note: Port is defined as the left side when facing the bow. Vo- begins the contrasting term Vomocagi on the following row; the locally italicized opening fragment is retained.

runs.text: Parte deſtibordo que he a contraria.

lines.note: Vomocagi denotes starboard, the opposite side. The Portuguese deſtibordo is retained as the printed form rather than normalized.
Torikago is a birdcage. The capital initial is T, correcting OCR Foricago, and the historical Portuguese Gayola remains unchanged.
Torikai first describes finally feeding a falcon fully. The Portuguese co- continues comer on the next line, while the Japanese principal forms retain their carons.

runs.text: mer ao falcão quanto quer, de pois que por vezes

lines.note: The falcon is allowed as much food as it wants after repeated smaller feeds. The printed separation de pois is preserved.

runs.text: lheforão dando pouco a pouco pera o fazer ca-

lines.note: The smaller portions were used gradually to train the bird to hunt. The physical ca- continues caçar below; the close-set lheforão follows the supplied reading.
After finishing caçar, inu wo torikoo applies the verb to training a dog. The scan clearly supports cão rather than OCR uão.

runs.text: pera a caça dos porcos pera que não tenha me-

lines.note: The dog is trained for hunting pigs so that it will not be afraid. The divided me- completes medo on the next row.

runs.text: do, ou das aues engodandoo com lhe dàr de co

lines.note: The definition also includes enticing the dog to hunt birds by feeding it. Comer is divided after co without a securely visible terminal hyphen, so none is supplied.

runs.text: mer, ou com lhe fazer tomar a caça morta,

lines.note: Completes comer and adds having the dog take dead game as another training method. The row remains part of the same long definition.
The figurative example hito wo torikoo concerns winning or enticing a person. En- begins Engodar, replacing the OCR fragment Et-.

runs.text: godar alguem dando lhealgũa couſa, ou fazẽ-

lines.note: The person is enticed by gifts or attentions. Godar completes Engodar, while fazẽ- begins the following verbal continuation; the terminal mark is a short hyphen.

runs.text: do lhe mimos pera o ter da ſua mão, &c.

lines.note: The favors are intended to keep the person under personal influence. The printed abbreviated fazẽ- plus do is retained without expanding its tilde.
Torikake means coming alongside to engage or attacking. The gloss continues the forceful-assault sense below.
The example teki ni torikakuru means rushing at enemies. The final to- begins the verb carried into the next row.
After completing torikakuru, a new example begins: torikakete kono koto wo. The object particle is uo in cotouo, not OCR toto; the sentence continues with iuaruru below.
Iwaruru completes the preceding example, translated as saying these things eagerly or impetuously. The printed Portuguese verb is Dezia, replacing OCR Dezta.
Adds with force or impetus to the manner of speaking. This closes the preceding usage example rather than defining a new word.
This separate torikake entry means beginning to pull something. The scan prints quru in the abbreviated paradigm; it is retained without regularizing the form to uru.
Completes dalgũa couſa, something from which one begins pulling. The word spans the line boundary without a supplied hyphen.
Torikarame means seizing or tying up. Both Portuguese alternatives describe restraint or binding.
Torikasane means adding or laying one thing upon another. The object continuation follows on the next row.
Completes the definition as one thing placed over another. The line belongs to torikasane and contains no separate entry.
Torikatame means keeping something strong or secure. The example begins Gin, a camp, fully visible at the right edge; the OCR Gi- truncates the printed n and invents a hyphen.
The alternative shiro wo torikatamuru concerns fortifying a castle. Portuguese arrayal refers to the camp; the final bẽ is an abbreviated bem, correcting OCR hẽ.
Completes the gloss: the camp is well arranged and fortified, or the fortress secured. The two objects correspond to Gin and Xiro in the Japanese example.

runs.text: Pelle que ſe poem nos punhos da

lines.note: Torikawa is leather placed on sword hilts. The Portuguese construction continues with Catana on the next physical row.

Catana completes the sword-hilt definition and occurs as a Japanese sword-name inside the Portuguese explanation. Its printed italic is retained and the whole word is flagged for optional typeface review.
Torikawashi means giving or exchanging between one another. The crop shows final ſi, not OCR ſu; the pronoun is separated from entre.
Completes the object of the exchange: some thing. This continuation is distinct from the following related verb.

Torikaye means changing or exchanging, with examples continuing at the top of the next page. The initial is capital T; the close-set trocarcomo is retained, and the lower veſtidos is a catchword rather than another body row.
